summary: Defines RADIUS attributes that give Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) support for IEEE 802.16 Privacy Key Management Version 1. These carry key-management information between the access network and the authentication server. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A wireless network and its door guard need a shared way to talk about keys. This defines the words they use.

subtitle: RADIUS attributes for securing wireless broadband subscriptions

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.16 fixed wireless broadband networks need to authenticate subscriber stations and exchange encryption keys, but RADIUS servers do not have a standard way to carry this key management information.
tldr.mechanism: Seven new RADIUS attributes are defined to carry certificates, configuration settings, cryptographic suites, security association identifiers, and encryption keys between the access network and the authentication server.
tldr.outcome: This enables RADIUS servers to manage key establishment and maintenance for 802.16 networks using PKMv1 protocol.

today: RFC 5904 remains the standard for RADIUS support of IEEE 802.16 PKMv1. It is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Authentication and Keys in Wireless Networks
sections.content:
IEEE 802.16 defines fixed wireless broadband systems where a Base Station communicates with Subscriber Stations. Privacy Key Management Version 1 (PKMv1) is a public-key-based protocol that lets the Base Station authenticate each subscriber and establish encryption keys for their traffic. PKMv1 uses X.509 certificates and RSA encryption to prove the identity of both the Base Station and the subscriber.

In many networks, authentication is delegated to a separate RADIUS server (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service), which manages user credentials and authorization policies. However, RADIUS was designed for dial-up networks and does not have standard attributes for PKMv1's key management information. This document defines those attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: A wireless tower and an office computer with passwords need to talk about who can connect and what secret codes to use. RADIUS is the translator, but it did not have the right words for wireless keys. These are the new words.

sections.title: The Seven RADIUS Attributes
sections.content:
This RFC defines seven new RADIUS attributes, assigned type numbers 137 through 143. The PKM-SS-Cert attribute carries the Subscriber Station's X.509 certificate. Because certificates can exceed RADIUS's maximum attribute size of 255 octets, large certificates are split across multiple attributes and reassembled by the server.

The PKM-CA-Cert attribute similarly carries the Certification Authority's certificate that signed the subscriber's certificate. The PKM-Config-Settings attribute is exactly 30 octets and bundles seven timeout values that control PKMv1 behavior, such as authentication wait times, re-authentication delays, and grace periods.

The PKM-Cryptosuite-List attribute specifies which encryption algorithms are available. The PKM-SAID attribute (4 octets) identifies a Security Association by a numeric identifier. The PKM-SA-Descriptor attribute (8 octets) packages a Security Association identifier with its type and cryptographic suite. Finally, the PKM-AUTH-Key attribute (135 octets) carries the authorization key, encrypted under the subscriber's public key using RSA encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of these as seven different envelopes. One holds the subscriber's ID card, one holds the CA's card, one lists what encryption codes are okay, one marks which agreement is which. The last one holds the secret key locked with the subscriber's personal lock.

sections.title: How the Attributes Are Used
sections.content:
When a Subscriber Station requests access, it sends an Access-Request message containing its certificate in one or more PKM-SS-Cert attributes and the CA certificate in PKM-CA-Cert attributes. It may also include the list of supported cryptographic suites and a Security Association identifier.

The RADIUS server processes these attributes, validates the certificates, and generates encryption keys. It responds with an Access-Accept message that includes the PKM-Config-Settings to tell the Base Station what timeouts to use, one or more PKM-SA-Descriptor attributes to describe the security associations, and the encrypted PKM-AUTH-Key. The authorization key itself must also be conveyed to the Base Station; the RFC recommends encapsulating it in the MS-MPPE-Send-Key attribute for protection.
sections.plainLanguage: The subscriber station says 'here's my ID and my encryption options.' The RADIUS server checks them and sends back 'okay, here are the timeout rules and your secret key.'

sections.title: Security Concerns
sections.content:
RADIUS as a protocol has known vulnerabilities discussed in RFC 3579. The cryptosuite list is particularly sensitive: if an attacker can modify it without detection, they might force weak encryption or disable encryption entirely. Similarly, if the authorization key attribute is not protected during transmission, an attacker could replace it with a key under their control, compromising the entire session.

The PKM-AUTH-Key attribute must always be accompanied by the Message-Authenticator attribute to ensure its integrity. Additionally, the document recommends that the authorization key sent to the Base Station be protected with strong encryption beyond standard RADIUS protection, noting that the MS-MPPE-Send-Key method has known weaknesses documented in RFC 3579.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone on the network could try to swap out the secret key or change the allowed encryption codes. The RADIUS server needs to use special tricks to make sure no one tamperes with these messages.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 5904 is an Informational specification published in June 2010. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the standard definition of how to extend RADIUS for IEEE 802.16 PKMv1 support. The attributes are registered with IANA and available for implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: This is still the official rulebook for these envelopes. It is not a candidate to become an official Internet Standard, but it is the published answer to the problem.
